title: Wings like eagles (Isaiah 40:28–31)
hookLine: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength

cards: It's mile twenty of a marathon. The crowds have thinned out. Legs that felt light at the start now feel like wet sand.

Runners call it the wall, and even the young, fit ones hit it. Now stretch that wall across years instead of miles. That's where the people Isaiah speaks to are: worn down by a long, long wait for something to change.
Some are saying out loud that God has forgotten them, that their cause has slipped past his notice. The same chapter that opened with comfort ends by answering them.

teach.b: First the prophet asks, almost impatient: "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?"

The one who made everything doesn't run out, and he gives power to the faint. Even young people get tired, Isaiah says; even strong young men stumble and fall. Strength isn't a matter of being young or fit.

Then the line people have stitched onto pillows and painted on locker-room walls: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."
Two things to notice. First, wait. The Hebrew word leans toward hope; some translations render it those who hope in the Lord.
It's leaning toward God, the way you lean toward a door when you hear the car pull in. Second, renew.
The Hebrew verb can also mean to change or exchange, and some readers hear a trade: spent strength for new. And look at the order: fly, then run, then walk.

teach.h: FLY, RUN, WALK: IT GOES DOWN.
teach.b: It goes down, not up. You might expect the big finish to be soaring.

teach.h: THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS AS EAGLES.
teach.b: Instead it ends with walking and not fainting. Some readers call that the honest part. Some days soar.
Some days run. And plenty of days, the gift is to walk and not faint. That may be why people carry this verse into hospital rooms and funerals: it doesn't promise flying every day.

how: Christians often memorize Isaiah 40:31, and it is frequently read at funerals and shared with people facing illness or exhaustion; it also appears in many hymns and worship songs.

o: a guard who keeps watch on the city wall
a desert wind that dries up the crops
the great bird Isaiah's tired people soar like

games.q: what's inside the promise — tap the pairs.

s: the verse builds up from walking to running to flying
it goes down: mount up, run, then walk and not faint.
waiting on the Lord, in this verse, means sitting idle
the Hebrew carries hope: leaning toward God with expectation.
Isaiah says even young people grow tired
even the youths faint and are weary; strength isn't about being young.

games.q: you're an exile, years into the wait, and you're exhausted. what does Isaiah say renews strength?
o: give up on the hope of home.
games.why: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength." not more effort: leaning toward God, and trading spent strength for new.

practice: Let your body be heavy, shoulders dropped, hands loose, feet flat, and notice where you're tired, your eyes, your back, your heart, without pushing past it.
Then simply wait, leaning toward God or toward stillness, expecting nothing in particular, breathing out the spent strength and breathing in as if trading it for new.
If you pray, you can say the line slowly: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength.

wordCard.voice: Nesher. Hebrew for the great bird translated eagle, Isaiah's promise to the tired: those who wait on God exchange their strength, and soar, and run, and keep walking.

orig.note: Hebrew: the great bird usually translated eagle. some scholars think it can also mean the griffon vulture.

carryVoice: Your line: fly, then run, then walk. On the slow days, walking counts. See you tomorrow.
